explanations: luna: The section describes a downward fall that can follow heedlessness; 2:36 says Satan caused Adam and his wife to slip from the Garden and they were sent down, a fall caused by temptation. | terra: Satan causes the pair to slip from the garden, brings them out of their state, and they are told to descend; deceptive prompting becomes an actual downward displacement.
luna: The section turns from falling to an upward summons; after the descent in 2:36, 2:38 promises that following God's guidance will leave no fear or grief.
luna: The section describes a companion whose influence ends at Hell; 2:166 shows leaders disowning their followers when they see punishment and their ties breaking.
luna: The section's falling person cannot be saved by what he has; 2:167 shows the followers wishing to return so they could disown their leaders, extending the failed-companionship scene.

luna: The section presents giving wealth as the upward path; 2:177 defines righteousness by giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, and freeing captives. | terra: Righteousness includes giving loved wealth, freeing slaves, and culminates in calling such people the Godfearing; it joins the ascent of 90:13 with the source’s giving ٱلْأَتْقَى.

terra: In the setting of spending, the command not to cast yourselves into destruction gives the section’s definition “exposing oneself to ruin” an ethical counterpart: give and do good rather than throw yourself over the edge.
terra: The associators call toward the Fire, while God calls toward the Garden and forgiveness; the section’s opposed directions become two explicit invitations.
luna: The section's image gives two opposed directions; 2:257 describes God bringing believers from darkness to light while false allies bring others from light into darkness, ending in the Fire.

luna: The section says the giver has no favor to repay and spends seeking God's face; 2:262 describes spending without following it with reminders or harm, a specific form of giving without an imposed debt.
luna: The section's giver acts without expectation of repayment; 2:263 says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, sharpening the boundary around sincere giving.
luna: The section gives wealth to purify oneself and seek God's face; 2:264 warns that showy spending and reminders can nullify charity, the opposite intention.

luna: The section's ascent is giving wealth toward the Lord Most High; 2:265 depicts spending to seek God's approval as a garden on elevated ground that produces abundantly, joining charity and elevation. | terra: Those who spend seeking God’s pleasure are like a garden on elevated ground; the act of giving and the physical height become one image of secure increase.
luna: The section says wealth cannot arrest a fall; 2:266 pictures a person's garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when he is old and weak, a precise loss of provision that cannot be undone.

luna: The section says wealth is given solely in seeking the Lord's face; 2:272 connects spending good to the spender and explicitly locates the expenditure in seeking God's face. | terra: The ayah says worthy expenditure is made seeking only God’s Face, directly matching the source giver’s motive in facing the Most High.

luna: The section says wealth cannot rescue a person from the fall; 3:10 says disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail them against God and identifies them as fuel for the Fire. | terra: The disbelievers’ wealth and children will not avail them against God, and they become fuel for the Fire; failed resources lead directly to burning.

terra: تَعَالَوْا summons both sides and their families to the decisive mutual invocation after knowledge has come; it exemplifies the call-form derived from height, though its immediate scene is disputation.

luna: The section names root ع ل و (B006) as a summons toward a high place; 3:64 uses that invitation form to call the People of Scripture to a common word of worshipping God alone. | terra: تَعَالَوْا calls the People of the Book to a common word of worshipping God alone; the source dictionary’s “come upward” form becomes a summons from false lordship to the true Lord.

luna: The section makes giving wealth part of turning upward; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves, specifying the cost of that orientation. | terra: People do not attain true righteousness until they spend from what they love, making relinquishment of cherished wealth the upward passage into virtue.

luna: The section's man approaches a well-mouth and falls; 3:103 recalls people at the edge of a fiery pit whom God rescued, reversing the image from an unhelped plunge to deliverance. | terra: The believers had stood on the lip of a pit of fire and God rescued them from it, directly staging the section’s person drawn safely away from the well-mouth.
terra: Wealth and children do not avail the disbelievers against God, and they are companions of the Fire; it repeats the section’s useless possession and fiery destination.
luna: The section's upward direction leads away from Fire; 3:133 calls believers to hasten toward forgiveness and a Garden prepared for the mindful.
luna: The section makes giving wealth part of the ascent; 3:134 identifies the mindful by spending in ease and hardship, restraining anger, and forgiving people.
terra: Believers are told not to weaken or grieve because they are ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ if faithful; true height is made conditional on faith rather than possession or self-claim.
terra: The hypocrites are told تَعَالَوْا to fight in God’s way or defend, but profess inability and retreat; the upward-form call discloses their contrary direction.

luna: The section says holding wealth cannot protect the falling person and commends giving; 3:180 warns those who withhold what God gave them that the hoarded wealth will be fastened around their necks.
terra: Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has succeeded; this is the closest nonlexical formulation of the source’s Godfearing person being moved aside from the blaze.

luna: The section names root ج ن ب (B003) for being turned aside; 4:31 uses its avoidance sense for major sins and connects that avoidance to forgiveness and an honorable entrance. | terra: Avoiding the major sins brings expiation and an honorable entrance, so an active use of the ج ن ب family leads beyond danger to a safe destination.

luna: The section's named root ع ل و (B006) makes coming a summons upward; 4:61 calls people to God's revelation and the Messenger, then depicts hypocrites turning away from the summons. | terra: When told تَعَالَوْا to God’s revelation and the Messenger, hypocrites turn away; the upward call and the refusing downward orientation are staged together.
terra: Those who strive with wealth and lives are favored by a degree over those who sit back, again attaching upward rank to the active surrender of possessions.
terra: Hypocrites occupy the lowest depth of the Fire, locating moral duplicity at the bottom of the section’s vertical axis.

luna: The section names root ر د ي (B003) for falling into a well and exposure to ruin; 5:3 uses its related form for an animal killed by falling, making the physical fall explicit while changing its cause and victim. | terra: ٱلْمُتَرَدِّيَةُ is an animal killed by a fall; this concrete legal use of ر د ي preserves the bodily plunge inside the source ayah’s moral ruin.
luna: The section's good direction seeks the Lord's pleasure and avoids ruin; 5:16 says those who follow God's pleasure are guided to paths of peace and brought from darkness to light.

terra: Believers are told to avoid intoxicants, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows so that they may succeed; ٱجْتَنِبُوهُ turns stepping aside from a snare into a commanded path to safety.

terra: The call تَعَالَوْا to revelation and the Messenger is refused for inherited custom even when the fathers lacked knowledge and guidance, showing what keeps people from answering the upward summons.
terra: Whoever has punishment turned away from him that Day has received mercy, a direct nonlexical equivalent of being moved aside from the threatened fire.
luna: The section turns the seeker toward the Lord's face; 6:52 describes humble people calling on their Lord morning and evening while seeking His face, whom the Messenger must not drive away.

luna: The section's worldly companion nearly pulls the speaker toward Hell; 6:71 depicts someone lured away by devils and confused while companions call him back to God's guidance, making the choice of direction explicit.
luna: The section says the falling person's wealth cannot help him; 6:94 depicts each person returning to God alone, having left behind what was given and losing the intercessors once trusted.

luna: The section presents highness as the direction of guidance; 6:125 uses climbing into the sky as an image of the constriction of misguidance, a useful limit showing that upward motion in the section is moral orientation rather than literal altitude. | terra: The person God leaves to stray experiences a constricted chest as though laboriously climbing into the sky; ascent becomes suffocation when it lacks guidance.

luna: The section names root ع ل و (B006) for the call to come to a high place; 6:151 uses that call to gather listeners for the Lord's ethical prohibitions. | terra: The Prophet says تَعَالَوْا and calls hearers to listen to what their Lord has forbidden; the dictionary form identified in the section introduces a concrete summons into divine guidance.
luna: The section's call upward establishes a direction; after the invitation to hear God's commands in 6:151, 6:153 names God's straight path and warns against diverging roads.
terra: God makes people successors on earth and raises some in degrees over others to test them in what He has given, turning possession and rank into examination rather than rescue.
luna: The section contrasts the downward fall with the upward face turned to God; 7:12 has Iblis claim superiority over Adam, showing a creature's false self-elevation.

luna: The section's false height ends below; after Iblis's boast in 7:12, 7:13 commands him to descend because of his arrogance. | terra: Satan is ordered to descend because arrogance has no place in the garden; attempted self-height directly produces abasement and downward removal.
luna: The section names a foot-snare as a secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005); 7:16 depicts Satan waiting in ambush on God's straight path, a specific lure away from the safe direction.

luna: The section's dictionary image of a foot-snare suggests a trap from which one must be kept away; after 7:16, 7:17 has Satan describe how he will approach people from every direction to divert them.

luna: The section says the fall has a blindness; 7:27 warns Adam's children that Satan and his tribe see them from where they cannot see, recalling the Garden's deceptive fall through an unseen enemy.
terra: A barrier separates the two destinations and men stand on the Heights recognizing each group, establishing the elevated threshold from which 7:47–48 look toward the Fire.
terra: When the people on the Heights have their eyes turned toward the people of the Fire, they pray not to be placed with them; this supplies the fearful downward gaze behind 7:48.
terra: From the Heights, men call to arrogant people and ask what their amassed company and pride availed them; height, downward recognition, and failed worldly resources converge here.
terra: The people once denied mercy by the arrogant are told to enter the Garden without fear or grief, reversing the judgment voiced by those whose gathering avails nothing in 7:48.

luna: The section's secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005) is a snare; 8:30 recounts a plot to seize, kill, or expel the Messenger and God's counter-plan, a concrete attempted capture that fails.
terra: Disbelievers spend wealth to bar others from God’s path, but their spending becomes regret, defeat, and gathering into Hell; expenditure pointed in the wrong direction cannot become ascent.
terra: Those who believe, migrate, and strive with wealth and lives are greater in rank with God, making devoted use of wealth an explicit elevation.

luna: The section contrasts wealth given for purification with wealth that cannot save; 9:34 condemns those who hoard gold and silver instead of spending it in God's way. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver rather than spend in God’s way are warned of painful punishment, setting stored wealth against the section’s purifying gift.

luna: The section links ruin to Fire; after 9:34's hoarded treasure, 9:35 says it will be heated in Hell and used to brand its owners. | terra: The hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, so the possession meant as security becomes the instrument of burning.
terra: God makes the disbelievers’ word the lowest while God’s word is the highest, ٱلْعُلْيَا; the section’s vertical axis becomes an explicit judgment between false and true claims.
terra: Someone asks to be spared a trial, yet the ayah says he has already fallen into it and Hell encompasses the disbelievers; the supposed escape is itself the hidden snare and fall.
terra: Some desert Arabs treat their spending as means of nearness to God and the Messenger’s prayers; wealth given away becomes actual approach rather than failed protection.
luna: The section describes giving wealth to purify oneself; 9:103 tells the Messenger to take charity from people's wealth to cleanse and purify them, giving that act a direct parallel.

luna: The section itself contrasts a structure collapsing into Hell with one founded on taqwa and riḍwān, roots it links to the surah's fifth and twenty-first verses; the unstable edge makes the fall an image of a false foundation. | terra: A building founded on taqwa and God’s pleasure stands opposite one on a collapsing cliff that carries its builder into Hell; the ayah contains the section’s foundation, brink, fall, and fiery end in one scene.

luna: The section says wealth is spent seeking the Lord's face and a higher outcome; 9:111 depicts God purchasing believers' selves and wealth in return for the Garden, recasting possession as directed toward the final home.
terra: God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, stating the safe destination of the true call in positive terms.
terra: Every wrongdoing soul would offer all the earth as ransom on seeing the punishment, a repeated formulation of possession failing at the decisive instant.
terra: Few believe Moses for fear of persecution because Pharaoh is high-handed in the land and excessive; claimed earthly height functions by pushing others down.
luna: The section depicts false elevation ending in a fall; 10:90 recounts Pharaoh and his people pursued into the sea and overwhelmed by drowning.
luna: The section warns that a fall leaves no time to reverse course; after drowning overtakes him, 10:91 rebukes Pharaoh's late profession of belief after prior disobedience.
luna: The section contrasts the fall with a warning that can still be seen; after Pharaoh's drowning in 10:90-91, 10:92 says his body is preserved as a sign for later people.
terra: Noah’s son trusts a mountain to protect him from the water, but no protector exists from God’s decree and the wave takes him; apparent physical height cannot arrest the fatal descent.

terra: Joseph’s brother proposes placing him in the hidden depth of a well, directly activating the well-mouth object behind the source dictionary definition, though Joseph is thrown rather than heedlessly falling.

luna: The section's plunge begins at a well; 12:15 recounts Joseph's brothers deliberately lowering him into a well, while God's inspiration preserves him, a descent with a different outcome from ruin. | terra: The brothers carry out their agreement to put Joseph in the well’s hidden depth; the image supplies the downward destination without making it his moral ruin.

luna: The section's well is a downward opening; 12:19 has a water-drawer raise Joseph from a well, reversing the direction and showing that a descent need not be the final end. | terra: A caravan lowers its bucket and draws Joseph out as found treasure; upward rescue from the literal well reverses the source image of an unrecoverable fall.

luna: The section names a foot-snare as a secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005); in 12:33 Joseph asks God to turn him from the women's plot rather than incline toward it, a specific lure he fears being caught by.

luna: The section depicts the mindful person being turned away from Fire; after Joseph asks for protection from the women's plot in 12:33, 12:34 says his Lord answered and turned their scheme away from him.

luna: The section says no wealth helps at the fall; 13:18 pictures the wrongdoer wishing to ransom himself with everything on earth and its like, but facing an evil reckoning and Hell. | terra: Those who do not answer their Lord would offer all the earth and as much again as ransom, yet face the bad reckoning and Hell; total possession cannot purchase removal from the end.
terra: Those who remain patient seeking their Lord’s Face and spend from His provision are promised the final abode, combining motive, giving, and destination.
luna: The section's deceiving companion leads toward ruin; 14:21 stages followers and arrogant leaders before God, where the leaders cannot offer the rescue their followers seek.
luna: The section's companion can pull someone toward destruction; 14:22 has Satan disown those who followed his invitation, specifying the betrayal after the lure.
luna: The section's axis sets descent against an upward turn; 14:24 compares a good word to a tree firmly rooted with branches high in the sky.
luna: The section's upward path bears a lasting result; 14:25 says the good tree gives fruit at all times by its Lord's permission.
luna: The section contrasts a stable foundation with a collapse; 14:26 compares a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability.
luna: The section's direction turns toward the Lord Most High; 14:27 says God keeps believers firm in this life and the Hereafter while wrongdoers are left astray.
luna: The section says wealth cannot be held back until the fall and directs it toward God; 14:31 urges believers to spend from their provision before the Day when no trade or friendship can help.
terra: Abraham asks God, وَٱجْنُبْنِى, to keep him and his sons away from worshipping idols; the source root ج ن ب retains its causative sense of making a person stand apart from danger.

luna: The section's unstable mosque falls from its foundation; 16:26 recounts earlier plotters whose building was torn from its foundations and whose roof fell over them, a matching collapse that exposes the plot. | terra: God attacks plotters’ building at its foundations so the roof falls on them from above; fabricated security becomes the mechanism of its owner’s collapse.

terra: Every community received the call to worship God and avoid false powers, after which the ayah contrasts those God guided with those upon whom error became due; stepping aside divides the two outcomes.
terra: Those who plot evil are asked whether they feel secure from God causing the earth to swallow them or punishment arriving unexpectedly; heedless security stands directly over a hidden fall.
terra: The heavenly servants fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded, giving divine height an answering posture of obedience rather than self-elevation.
terra: Israel is warned that it will corrupt twice and rise to great self-exaltation, using عُلُوًّا for a height whose very form invites judgment.
terra: The ayah says the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preferment than worldly differentiation, relocating true elevation beyond present possessions.
luna: The section juxtaposes a fall below with the Lord Most High; 17:37 sets a boundary on human height, saying a person cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height.
terra: God is glorified and exalted in immense height above what people falsely attribute to Him, reserving true عُلُوّ for God rather than human claimants.
terra: Those delivered to land are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed into it or struck by a storm with no guardian, repeating the brink hidden beneath ordinary safety.
luna: The section's fall carries blindness toward Fire; 17:97 depicts people gathered blind, mute, and deaf on their faces, with Hell as their refuge.
luna: The section says wealth is given only in seeking the Lord's face; 18:28 describes people who call on their Lord seeking His face and warns against turning one's eyes toward worldly adornment.
terra: The believing companion warns that the rich man’s garden may become a bare slippery ground, foreshadowing the collapse of owned security in 18:42.
terra: He also warns that its water may sink so deep that the owner cannot retrieve it; apparent command of property ends at an inaccessible depth.

luna: The section's wealth cannot arrest a fall; in 18:42 a garden's trellises collapse over its owner and he wrings his hands over what he spent, making material possession fail amid physical collapse. | terra: The rich man’s produce is destroyed and his trellises lie collapsed while he regrets what he spent on them; possessed wealth and its supporting structure fail together.

luna: The section says the falling man's wealth cannot help him; after the garden collapses in 18:42, 18:43 says he has no group to help him against God, completing the helplessness. | terra: After the garden’s collapse, he has no party to help him apart from God and cannot help himself, echoing the source’s insistence that what is in the falling man’s hand cannot arrest ruin.
luna: The section turns from failed worldly wealth to seeking the Lord's face; after the ruined garden in 18:42, 18:44 locates true protection and the best outcome with God.
luna: The section depicts a ruin from which wealth cannot rescue a person; 18:53 says wrongdoers will see the Fire and know they are falling into it, with no way to turn aside.

luna: The section contrasts a failing structure with one grounded in righteousness and says the giver expects no repayment; 18:77 depicts a wall about to collapse being set upright, with payment explicitly waived as a possible alternative.
luna: The section says the giver has no favor to collect; after the wall is repaired in 18:77, 18:82 reveals it protected the treasure of two orphans until they mature, explaining the unpaid act.
terra: God raises Idris to مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا, a high station; this is a positive personal elevation from the same ع ل و family, though without the source’s brink scene.

luna: The section distinguishes between entering the Fire and being kept away; 19:71 says all come to it, setting the boundary that 19:72 draws. | terra: Everyone is brought to Hell according to the Lord’s decree, establishing the perilous threshold from which 19:72 specifically saves the Godfearing.

luna: The section's God-fearing person is kept away from the Fire; after 19:71 says all come to it, 19:72 says God saves the mindful and leaves wrongdoers there on their knees. | terra: God saves those who were Godfearing and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling there, closely paralleling ٱلْأَتْقَى being removed from the Fire while its opposite remains.
luna: The section exposes wealth as no protection at ruin; 19:77 depicts a denier boasting that he will be given wealth and children, the false security challenged in the next verses.
luna: The section says no worldly possession secures the final outcome; after the boast in 19:77, 19:78 challenges whether the speaker knows the unseen or has a promise from God.
luna: The section's falling man cannot use wealth to escape consequence; 19:79 says the boast will be recorded and punishment extended.
luna: The section says possessions cannot accompany the person in ruin; 19:80 says God will inherit what the speaker claims and he will come alone.

luna: The section names root ر د ي (B003) for falling and facing ruin; in 20:16 Moses is warned that following desire away from the Hour will make him perish, turning the fall into the consequence of heedless deviation. | terra: Moses is warned not to let a denier who follows desire turn him from the Hour, فَتَرْدَىٰ; the same ر د ي root makes heedless appetite a route to destruction.
terra: God tells the fearful Moses that he is ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ, turning height into divine reassurance before confrontation with deceptive power.
terra: The believer who comes with righteous deeds receives ٱلدَّرَجَـٰتُ ٱلْعُلَىٰ, “the highest degrees”; moral action ends in the height signified by the source root ع ل و.
terra: Israel is warned not to transgress over its good provision lest wrath descend, and whoever incurs that wrath has fallen; moral excess, downward movement, and ruin are made explicit.
luna: The section's falling danger includes being drawn away by another; 20:117 warns Adam that Satan is an enemy who would expel him from the Garden and make him wretched.
terra: After the command to descend, God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither stray nor suffer; guidance marks the route that prevents descent from becoming ruin.

luna: The section warns of falling into fire; in 21:68 Abraham's opponents order that he be burned, setting up the reversal in the next ayah. | terra: Abraham’s opponents command that he be burned to support their gods; the intended fiery trap is the one God overturns in 21:69.

luna: The section contrasts entering fire with being kept away from it; 21:69 makes the fire cool and safe for Abraham, reversing the fire's destructive action in the preceding verse. | terra: God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, showing that the apparent fiery snare has no power over the person whom God preserves.

luna: The section contrasts a fall into ruin with protection; after the failed attempt to burn Abraham in 21:68-69, 21:70 says the plotters were made the losers. | terra: The plotters intend harm, but God makes them the greatest losers; the agents who prepare another’s destruction inherit the downward outcome.

luna: The section says the most mindful person will be kept away from the Fire; 21:101 likewise says those for whom God's good promise has gone ahead are kept far from it. | terra: Those for whom the best decree has preceded are kept far away from Hell, a direct semantic parallel to the Godfearing person being pulled aside from it.

luna: The section depicts safety from the Fire; after 21:101 says the promised ones are kept far away, 21:102 adds that they will not hear its faintest sound, describing the distance's result. | terra: Those kept far from Hell do not even hear its sound and remain amid what they desire, showing the completeness of the removal asserted in 21:101.
terra: One who worships on an edge reverses himself when tested and loses both worlds; unstable worship turns the brink into the face-first reversal imagined by the section.
terra: The command to avoid the pollution of idols and false speech uses the source’s ج ن ب family for deliberate removal from what corrupts.

luna: The section pictures a man tumbling down and sets descent against an upward turn; 22:31 likens associating partners with God to falling from the sky, snatched by birds or swept far away by wind, giving the downward direction a spiritual meaning. | terra: The associator is likened to one fallen from the sky, then snatched by birds or hurled far by wind; this is an exposed, irrecoverable plunge into destruction.

luna: The section sets a well-mouth below against the Lord Most High; 22:45 describes ruined towns with abandoned wells and lofty palaces, placing low and high structures together in a landscape of collapse.

luna: The section says the fall has a blindness of its own; after 22:45's ruined wells and palaces, 22:46 clarifies that the blindness is in hearts, not eyes, connecting heedlessness with the descent.
terra: Because God is the Truth and what is invoked besides Him is false, the ayah names God as the High and Great; true height is explicitly bounded against false worship.
terra: Pharaoh and his chiefs respond arrogantly to Moses and Aaron and are called a people who were عَالِينَ; height names oppressive refusal rather than nearness to God.
luna: The section contrasts one who turns away with one who faces the Lord; 24:48 depicts a group turning aside when called to God and the Messenger for judgment.
luna: The section's upward direction is a response to guidance; after 24:48's refusal, 24:51 depicts believers hearing and obeying when called to God and the Messenger.
luna: The section portrays a companion nearly pulling someone into ruin; 25:27 shows a wrongdoer biting his hand in remorse when consequences arrive, with the cause explained in the next two ayat.

luna: The section's falling man can be led toward destruction by another; 25:28 names the wrongdoer's regret at having taken a certain person as a friend. | terra: The wrongdoer wishes he had not taken a certain person as an intimate friend, echoing the garden-dweller’s recognition that a companion nearly caused his fall.

luna: The section says a companion can nearly bring someone to ruin; 25:29 says that friend turned him away from the Reminder after it came, specifying the lure's effect. | terra: The regretted companion led him away from the Reminder after it reached him, and Satan proves deserting; this identifies diversion from guidance as the mechanism of the fall in 25:28.
terra: The servants of the Merciful ask that Hell’s punishment be turned away from them, voicing the movement away from fire that source وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا promises.

luna: The section says wealth cannot secure the falling person and directs giving toward God's face; 26:88 says wealth and children will not benefit on the Day. | terra: On the Day of Resurrection neither wealth nor children benefit, giving the source’s “wealth does not avail” its final-day scope.
luna: The section opposes empty wealth to sincere orientation toward the Lord's face; 26:89 names a sound heart as the exception to 26:88's failed wealth.
terra: The false gods and the strayers are tumbled headlong into Hell, a direct infernal version of the source’s rolling fall.
terra: Solomon writes, “Do not exalt yourselves over me; come to me in submission”; self-height from the ع ل و root is answered by a summons that requires surrender.
terra: Whoever brings a good deed receives better and is secure from that Day’s terror, supplying the protected counterpart to the face-first casting in 27:90.
terra: Those bringing evil are cast face-first into the Fire, a concise infernal enactment of downward direction and the unprotected face.
terra: Pharaoh عَلَا in the land and divided its people, so the root ع ل و denotes oppressive self-elevation rather than the true height sought in the source.

luna: The section exposes a false claim to the highest lordship; 28:38 has Pharaoh claim divinity and ask for a tower from which to look toward Moses' God, pairing the claim with an attempted ascent. | terra: Pharaoh orders a tower built so he may ascend toward Moses’ God while asserting no other deity; fabricated physical ascent exposes the falsity of his claim to height.
luna: The section's false high claimant is brought down; after Pharaoh's tower claim in 28:38, 28:40 says he and his army were seized and cast into the sea.

luna: The section says orientation ends either upward or in ruin; 28:41 depicts Pharaoh's leaders as calling to the Fire and lacking help on the Day. | terra: Pharaoh and his chiefs are made leaders who call to the Fire and receive no help on Judgment Day, presenting false leadership as a downward summons.
luna: The section turns wealth toward the Lord's higher face; 28:77 tells Qarun to use what God gave him to seek the Hereafter, connecting provision to a higher end.
luna: The section says wealth cannot keep someone from a fall; after the counsel in 28:77, Qarun claims his riches came from his own knowledge, a self-reliance exposed by his later destruction.
luna: The section contrasts worldly possessions with seeking the Lord Most High; 28:79 shows Qarun displaying his adornments, the spectacle that makes people wish for his position.
luna: The section directs the reader toward a higher reward rather than wealth; after Qarun's display in 28:79, people of knowledge say God's reward is better for those who believe and do right.

luna: The section says wealth cannot help the man when he falls; 28:81 describes Qarun and his home swallowed by the earth, with no company able to help him, making that claim concrete in the case of a rich man. | terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed into the earth, and neither his party nor he can save him; his great property and support are powerless at a literal downward ruin.

luna: The section says wealth cannot help the one who falls; after Qarun is swallowed in 28:81, 28:82 shows those who envied his position recognizing that God distributes provision as He wills. | terra: Those who had desired Qarun’s station recognize after his swallowing that worldly provision is no proof of success; the witnessed fall corrects their valuation of wealth.

luna: The section exposes Pharaoh's false claim to highness; 28:83 says the Hereafter belongs to those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth. | terra: The final home is for those who do not desire عُلُوًّا, self-exaltation on earth; it distinguishes ascent toward the Most High from making oneself high over others.
luna: The section says wealth cannot help at ruin and directs the giver toward the Lord's face; 28:88 says everything perishes except God's Face, clarifying the lasting object of that orientation.
terra: Abraham’s people propose killing or burning him, but God saves him from the fire; deliberate casting is answered by divine removal.

terra: The summary of destroyed peoples includes one whom God caused the earth to swallow and insists none could escape the consequence of wrongdoing; Qarun’s fall becomes one form in a larger pattern of self-caused ruin.
terra: Punishment covers the wrongdoers from above and from beneath their feet, turning the root-family suggestion of a foot snare into complete vertical enclosure.

luna: The section directs giving toward the Lord's face; 30:38 names relatives, needy people, and travelers as recipients, then links giving to those who desire God's face and success. | terra: Giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their due is attributed to those who desire God’s Face; expenditure is again directed upward by its object of desire.
luna: The section contrasts a summons toward the highest with a downward end; 31:21 describes people rejecting what God revealed even when Satan calls them toward the punishment of the Blaze.
terra: The repeated declaration that God is Truth, rival invocations are false, and He is the High and Great reinforces who alone owns the section’s upward pole.

terra: The form تَعَالَيْنَ calls the Prophet’s wives to receive provision and a gracious release if they choose worldly life and adornment; it is a specific boundary case where the root-form “come” introduces separation, while 33:29 states the higher alternative.

terra: Choosing God, His Messenger, and the final home instead of worldly adornment completes the fork opened by تَعَالَيْنَ in 33:28 and clarifies which choice corresponds to the section’s upward orientation.
terra: The deniers are confronted with the earth below and sky above: God could make the earth swallow them or drop a fragment of sky; ruin can open in either vertical direction.
luna: The section says wealth does not save the person who falls; 34:35 depicts disbelievers trusting that abundant wealth and children mean they will not be punished.
luna: The section's wealthy man cannot rely on his possessions; after 34:35's boast, 34:36 says God expands and restricts provision as He wills, displacing the claim of self-made security.

luna: The section says wealth is given to purify oneself and seek God's face; 34:37 says wealth and children do not bring a person near to God, except faith and righteous action. | terra: Wealth and children do not bring people near to God, whereas faith and righteous action do; it explicitly separates owned means from the genuine upward approach.
luna: The section's companion nearly pulls someone toward Hell; 35:6 calls Satan an enemy who invites his own faction to become companions of the Blaze.

luna: The section turns the reader upward toward the Lord Most High; 35:10 says good speech ascends to Him and righteous action raises it, making moral action a literal upward motion. | terra: Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, making orientation toward divine height a movement enacted by deeds.
terra: A barrier is set before and behind the rejecters and they are covered so they cannot see; blindness and confinement make continued movement itself perilous.
terra: The attendants are told to guide the wrongdoers and their associates to the path of Hell, a terrible counter-image in which “guidance” directs companions downward.
terra: A garden-dweller recalls that he had a close companion, identifying the person later seen below and accused in 37:56 of nearly causing his ruin.
terra: The speaker asks his companions whether they will look, initiating the downward view into Hell completed in 37:55.

luna: The section's downward direction culminates in a look below; 37:55 has the saved speaker look and see his former companion in Hell, supplying the view that 37:56's near-ruin recalls. | terra: The garden-dweller looks down and sees his companion in the middle of Hell; it supplies the high vantage and downward gaze that make the near-fall named in 37:56 visible.

luna: The section names root ر د ي (B003) for ruin by falling; 37:56 uses that root when the speaker says his worldly companion nearly ruined him, and 37:55 places that companion in Hell. | terra: The saved speaker tells his former companion, تَرْدِينِ, that he nearly caused his ruin; this is the same ر د ي fall as the source word تَرَدَّىٰ, now understood from above after a narrow escape.

luna: The section contrasts the one who falls with the one kept safe; after 37:56's near-disaster, the speaker credits his Lord's favor for not being among the punished, showing what turned him aside. | terra: The speaker credits his Lord’s grace for not being among those brought to punishment, completing 37:56’s claim that his foot was almost drawn into ruin but was spared.

luna: The section's fire is a destination of destruction; 37:97 has Abraham's people build a structure and cast him into a blaze, a direct fire scene whose outcome differs in 37:98. | terra: Abraham’s opponents propose building a structure and casting him into a blaze, deliberately constructing the fiery trap whose direction God reverses in 37:98.

luna: The section's pious person is kept away from fire; after Abraham is cast into it in 37:97, 37:98 says his opponents' scheme failed, completing the reversal. | terra: They intend a plot against Abraham, but God makes them the lowest, explicitly bringing the would-be burners down instead.

luna: The section contrasts true highness with a creature's pride; 38:75 rebukes Iblis for refusing to bow before Adam. | terra: God asks Iblis whether he has grown arrogant or counts himself among ٱلْعَالِينَ; the root of height is interrogated as a false status claimed against divine command.
luna: The section's vertical axis separates God's true height from self-asserted rank; 38:76 repeats Iblis's claim that he is better because he was made of fire while Adam was made of clay.
luna: The section depicts a false elevation ending in a fall; after Iblis's superiority claim in 38:76, 38:77 commands him to leave.
luna: The section turns from false highness to ruin; 38:78 places a curse on Iblis until the Day of Judgment after his rejection.

luna: The section names root ج ن ب (B003) for keeping someone away; 39:17 describes people who avoid false gods and turn to God, linking deliberate avoidance to good news. | terra: Those who avoid false powers rather than worship them and turn back to God receive good news; withdrawal from the false object is paired with orientation toward God.
terra: A person can only shield the face from the worst punishment, a posture showing that no possession or ordinary defense remains available at the fall.
terra: If the wrongdoers owned everything on earth and its equal, they would offer it against the Day’s punishment, showing wealth’s complete impotence only when ruin becomes visible.

luna: The section says the most mindful person is kept away from the Fire; 39:61 says God saves those who feared Him and no evil will touch them. | terra: God saves those with taqwa in their place of triumph, with evil neither touching nor grieving them; their precaution culminates in divine extraction from danger.
terra: The disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell until its gates open, giving the downward company and destination opposite the Godfearing group in 39:73.
terra: Those who feared their Lord are conducted in groups to the Garden, setting the Godfearing person’s destination opposite the fiery route without relying on possessions.
terra: The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds and say that whoever is protected that Day has received mercy; divine protection removes both the cause and outcome of the fall.
terra: God is the Raiser of degrees and Lord of the Throne, locating the power to confer true height in the same divine source toward which the section turns.

luna: The section's upward direction is a summons toward the Lord Most High; 40:36 has Pharaoh order a tower built so he can try to reach heaven and inspect Moses' God, an attempted ascent that confuses height with authority. | terra: Pharaoh asks Haman to build him a tower so he may reach the routes, beginning an attempted ascent toward the heavens that 40:37 exposes as delusion.

luna: The section distinguishes true elevation from a false claim; 40:37 says Pharaoh's tower plan only led to loss and that he was turned from the way. | terra: Pharaoh proposes looking upon Moses’ God from the tower, but his plot ends only in ruin; self-authorized ascent becomes another path to destruction.
terra: The believing man asks why he calls his people to salvation while they call him to the Fire; the rival calls state the section’s two directions without metaphor.
terra: His people call him to deny God and associate what he does not know, while he calls them to the Mighty, Forgiving One; the content of each direction in 40:41 is made explicit.

luna: The section's pious person is kept away from ruin; 40:45 says God protected a believing man from Pharaoh's people's evil plot. | terra: God protects the believing man from the evils of Pharaoh’s plots, while the next ayah says punishment encloses Pharaoh’s people; rescue and entrapment divide the two directions.

luna: The section makes Fire the end of a false direction; after the believer is protected in 40:45, 40:46 says Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening. | terra: Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening and then admitted to harsher punishment, completing 40:45’s reversal of plotter and protected believer.
luna: The section says a companion or leader cannot save the falling person; 40:47 depicts the weak and arrogant disputing in the Fire, continuing the fate of Pharaoh's people in 40:46.
terra: The disbelievers ask to see the human and jinn misleaders so they can put them beneath their feet among the lowest; the companions who caused error are assigned the downward place.
terra: The ayah asks whether one cast into the Fire is better or one who comes secure on Resurrection Day, directly setting involuntary fiery descent against safe arrival.
terra: The believers are characterized by avoiding major sins and indecencies and forgiving when angered; the source root describes a sustained moral position away from ruin.

terra: God distributes livelihoods and raises people over one another in degrees for mutual service, yet His mercy is better than what they amass; worldly height and accumulation are expressly relativized.

luna: The section describes a fall caused by heedless turning; 43:36 says one who turns away from the Reminder is assigned a devil as companion, joining the turn with a destructive guide. | terra: Whoever blinds himself to the Merciful’s remembrance is assigned a satan as a close companion, joining the section’s heedlessness to the dangerous companion scene.

luna: The section's companion pulls the unwary toward ruin; 43:37 says such companions divert people from the path while they think they are guided. | terra: Those companions bar people from the path while the people suppose themselves guided, making the plunge’s blindness a false confidence about direction.

luna: The section's near-fall is tied to a worldly companion; 43:38 has the deluded person wish for a great distance from that companion when both arrive before God. | terra: On coming before God, the misled person wishes an east-to-west distance separated him from the companion; only at the destination does he perceive how far the companion pulled him off course.
terra: Regret cannot help because wrongdoer and companion share the punishment, completing the hidden companionship trap of 43:36–38.

luna: The section contrasts the Lord Most High with a human claim to supremacy; 43:51 has Pharaoh boast of Egypt and the rivers flowing beneath him, grounding his claim in worldly height and power. | terra: Pharaoh proclaims his Egyptian kingdom and points to rivers flowing beneath him, staging his false lordship through an earthly above-and-below hierarchy.
luna: The section's false claimant draws others toward ruin; 43:54 says Pharaoh made his people disregard the truth and they obeyed him, showing the reach of his authority.

luna: The section says false elevation ends in being brought down; after Pharaoh's boast and his people's obedience, 43:55 says God took retribution on them. | terra: When Pharaoh’s people provoke God, all are drowned, turning the ruler who boasted of waters beneath him into one overwhelmed by water.
luna: The section turns from false height to a fall; 43:56 says Pharaoh and his people were drowned and made an example for later generations.
luna: The section's worldly friend nearly brings his companion to Hell; 43:67 reverses that relation by saying close friends become enemies on that Day except the mindful.
terra: God rescues Israel from Pharaoh’s humiliating torment and calls Pharaoh high-handed and excessive; the oppressor’s عَالِي status is set against divine rescue from beneath it.

luna: The section's most mindful person is kept from the Fire; 44:56 describes the people of the Garden as protected from Hell's punishment, a parallel final safety. | terra: The garden-dwellers taste no further death and God protects them from Hell’s punishment, restating the completed safety of one drawn away from fire.
terra: Believers are told not to lose heart while they are ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ and God is with them; the source root marks a conferred moral position rather than self-exaltation.
luna: The section contrasts a person kept away from Fire with the one who enters it; 50:31 says the Garden is brought near to the mindful, completing the other side of the destination.

luna: The section's pious person is turned aside from the Fire; 52:18 says the people of the Garden enjoy their provision while their Lord protects them from Hell's punishment. | terra: The garden-dwellers rejoice because their Lord protected them from the punishment of Hell, supplying the safe outcome after removal from the brink.

luna: The section's root ج ن ب (B003) describes keeping away; 53:32 applies it to avoiding major sins and indecencies, a specific form of the mindful separation in the section. | terra: Those who avoid the major sins and indecencies, apart from minor lapses, stand within the Lord’s vast forgiveness; avoidance is linked to mercy rather than mere spatial distance.

luna: The section warns of falling into Fire; 54:48 depicts disbelievers dragged into it on their faces, making the downward bodily motion explicit. | terra: Criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire; face, involuntary movement, and fiery ruin fuse as they do in the section’s use of 22:11.
luna: The section contrasts disposable worldly wealth with seeking the Lord's face; 55:26 says all on earth will perish, setting up what remains in 55:27.
luna: The section directs the giver toward the Lord's face; after 55:26 says all earthly things perish, 55:27 says the Face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains.
terra: The Event is “abasing, raising,” compressing the section’s two directions into the final reversal by which some are lowered and others elevated.
terra: Those who spent and struggled before the victory are greater in degree than later spenders, explicitly turning expenditure into an elevated rank.
terra: No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers, and the Fire is their refuge; the failed payment and fiery destination are explicitly joined.

luna: The section contrasts the low fall with the Lord Most High; 58:11 says God raises believers and those given knowledge by degrees, a direct moral use of elevation. | terra: God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees, explicitly making faithful response the cause of upward rank.
terra: Neither wealth nor children avail the opponents of God, and the ayah assigns them to the Fire; worldly protection proves unable to prevent the final descent.
terra: The Helpers prefer others despite their own need, and those protected from their soul’s greed succeed; being guarded from the inner snare is expressed through giving.
terra: Satan urges a person to disbelieve and then disowns him once he does, giving another specific instance of a companion leading someone toward ruin and abandoning him at the edge.
terra: The tempter and the tempted end together eternally in the Fire, completing 59:16’s false companionship with the destination it concealed.
luna: The section links giving wealth and mindful orientation to safety from ruin; 61:10 introduces a trade that saves believers from painful punishment.
luna: The section's upward turn involves giving wealth; 61:11 identifies belief and striving with wealth and selves as the saving trade introduced in 61:10.
luna: The section contrasts the Fire with being turned away from it; 61:12 gives the promised outcome of the saving trade as forgiveness and Gardens.

terra: When told تَعَالَوْا so the Messenger may seek forgiveness for them, the hypocrites turn their heads and withdraw arrogantly; refusal of the root’s upward call is itself a claim of false height.
luna: The section says wealth cannot help at the moment of falling; 63:9 warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering God.
luna: The section's wealth is spent toward God before ruin; after 63:9's warning, 63:10 urges spending before death arrives and a person asks for more time to give.
luna: The section warns that worldly wealth does not stop a fall; 63:11 says death cannot be delayed once its time comes, completing the warning to spend before it.
luna: The section says wealth cannot secure the person who falls; 64:15 calls wealth and children a trial, placing worldly possession beneath the great reward with God.

luna: The section contrasts the generous giver with the one who falls; 64:16 urges obedience and spending and says the person protected from greed is successful. | terra: The command joins taqwa, obedience, and spending, then names protection from one’s own greed as success; it maps the source Godfearing giver’s safe direction.
luna: The section's giver seeks a higher reward without a human debt; 64:17 promises multiplied reward and forgiveness for a good loan to God.
terra: Believers are commanded to guard themselves and their families from a Fire, converting the section’s rescue image into an imperative of prevention.

luna: The section develops a heedless approach to a hole; 67:16 warns people who feel secure that the earth may swallow them suddenly, making presumed safety itself part of the danger. | terra: People are asked whether they feel secure from the earth suddenly swallowing them; the unnoticed ground can become the pit beneath a confident walker.

luna: The section contrasts a man tumbling down with a person turned toward the highest; 67:22 directly contrasts one walking face-down with one upright on a straight path, making posture and guidance part of the same image. | terra: The ayah contrasts one walking fallen upon his face with one walking upright on a straight path; it is the section’s heedless walker and two directions rendered as rival postures.

luna: The section says a man's wealth does not avail him when he falls; in 69:28 the judged speaker says his wealth did not help him, a close formulation in its own reckoning scene. | terra: The condemned person says his wealth did not avail him, turning the source’s third-person verdict about useless property into the fallen person’s own recognition.

luna: The section says the falling man's possessions cannot save him; 69:29 adds that his authority has vanished, extending failed wealth to failed status. | terra: The condemned person says his authority has perished after admitting that wealth failed in 69:28; every secondary means of arresting the fall has vanished.

luna: The section's fall reveals helplessness; after the speaker's lost wealth and authority in 69:28-29, 69:30 orders him seized, showing the reversal of worldly power. | terra: The order to seize and shackle him removes freedom of movement immediately before the command to burn him in 69:31.

luna: The section links ruin to fire; after the seizure in 69:30, 69:31 sends the judged person into the Blaze. | terra: The command then says to make him enter and burn in Hell, so 69:28’s useless wealth culminates in the same fiery destination carried by source يَصْلَىٰهَا.

luna: The section's steep ascent is freeing a slave and feeding in hunger; 69:34 says the condemned person did not urge feeding the poor, a specific reversal tied to the Fire in the surrounding verses. | terra: The condemned person did not encourage feeding the needy, adding a withheld ascent-act to the useless wealth and burning already described in 69:28–31.
luna: The section says wealth cannot help the falling man; after the condemned person's failure to feed the poor in 69:34, 69:35 says he has no devoted friend to help him.
terra: God is Lord of the ascents, locating true upward ways with Him and preparing the actual ascent described in 70:4.
terra: The angels and Spirit ascend to God, supplying a cosmic literalization of the upward direction owned by the Lord of ascents in 70:3.
terra: The criminal would ransom himself from that Day with his children, beginning the exhaustive proof that no possessed human resource can stop the fiery outcome in 70:15.
terra: He would surrender his spouse and brother as ransom, extending the failed attempt to arrest ruin through what is closest to him.
terra: He would offer the clan that sheltered him, so even the social protection once surrounding him cannot pull him away.
terra: He would offer everyone on earth if that could save him, exhausting all imaginable ransom immediately before the ayah rejects escape and names the blaze.

luna: The section connects turning from guidance with the Fire; 70:15 introduces the blazing flame that seizes those described in the following verses. | terra: The punishment is لَظَىٰ, a blazing fire, recalling the source surah’s fiery setting and opening a sequence in which hoarded wealth ends there.

luna: The section's Fire is a destructive endpoint; 70:16 describes the flame stripping away, sharpening the consequence announced in 70:15. | terra: The blaze strips away the scalp, making the bodily exposure to ruin in 70:15 concrete rather than metaphorical.

luna: The section names the root ج ن ب (B003) for being turned aside from something; 70:17 says the flame calls the one who turned his back and turned away, the reverse of the mindful person being kept away from it. | terra: The blaze calls the one who turned his back and withdrew, a grim counter-call to the section’s summons upward toward the Most High.

luna: The section contrasts spending wealth to purify oneself with a ruinous descent; 70:18 completes the description of the flame's target as the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it. | terra: The person summoned by the blaze amassed wealth and stored it away, directly joining hoarding to the fiery end described in 70:15.
luna: The section sets the generous, God-fearing person against the one led to ruin; after the hoarder of 70:18, 70:22 introduces those who persist in prayer as an exception.
luna: The section's upward path includes giving wealth; 70:24 says the people of prayer recognize a due in their wealth, a concrete counterpart to the section's generous path.
luna: The section makes feeding the hungry part of the steep ascent; 70:25 specifies the needy and deprived as recipients of that due.
luna: The section presents a reminder for the one who fears; 70:27 describes the people of the upward path as fearing their Lord's punishment.
luna: The section contrasts the one entering Fire with the one turned away from it; after describing the God-fearing group in 70:22-34, 70:35 places them in honored Gardens.
terra: Whoever turns away from the Lord’s remembrance is driven into an escalating, arduous punishment; this difficult “ascent” reverses the source’s upward call.
terra: The condemned man is given extensive wealth, identifying the worldly resource that precedes the punitive ascent announced in 74:17.
terra: Despite abundant gifts, he greedily desires still more; possession does not change his direction and instead prepares the burden that follows.
terra: God will burden him with a punishing ascent, صَعُودًا; upward motion here is torment, a sharp reversal that prevents the section’s moral ascent from being reduced to mere height.
terra: God says He will make the rejecter burn in Saqar, using a ص ل ي verb after the wealthy man’s false security and punitive climb.

luna: The section distinguishes the Fire from the person kept away from it; 74:42 asks the condemned what brought them into Saqar, setting up their own account. | terra: The people of the right ask the criminals what put them into Saqar, opening the explanation of the fiery destination named in 74:26.
luna: The section's ascent is a path of mindful action; 74:43 names failure to pray among the condemned's reasons for entering Saqar.

luna: The section makes feeding the hungry part of the steep path; 74:44 gives failure to feed the poor as a reason for entering Saqar, the direct opposite. | terra: The criminals say they did not feed the needy, making refusal of the steep ascent’s feeding act one stated cause of their fiery destination.
luna: The section contrasts a God-fearing direction with ruin; 74:45 says the condemned joined in vain discourse, another part of their account of how they reached Saqar.
luna: The section's vertical choice ends in either safety or ruin; 74:46 says the people of Saqar denied the Day of Recompense.
luna: The section's falling ends in an irreversible consequence; 74:47 closes the account of Saqar with the certainty that finally came to its occupants.

luna: The section's upward path gives wealth away and feeds the hungry; 76:8 depicts righteous people giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, meeting the steep ascent’s concrete use of possessions.

luna: The section says the giving is only to seek the Lord's face, with no favor owed in return; 76:9 makes the feeding likewise free of any wish for reward or thanks. | terra: They explain that they feed only for God’s Face and want neither reward nor thanks, closely paralleling giving without repayment while seeking the Lord’s Face.
luna: The section calls this a reminder for the one who fears; 76:10 says the givers fear a severe day from their Lord.

luna: The section contrasts the Fire with the person kept from it; after the fear in 76:10, 76:11 says God protects the givers from that day's evil and gives them radiance and joy. | terra: God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day and grants radiance and joy; removal from danger opens into the positive state beyond it.
luna: The section presents Pharaoh's claim to be highest as a public false elevation; 79:23 shows him gathering and calling his people, the public setting for the claim in 79:24.

luna: The section names root ع ل و (B001) through الأعلى and points to Pharaoh's false claim; 79:24 has Pharaoh call himself the most high lord, a direct counterfeit of the section's Lord Most High. | terra: Pharaoh declares himself the people’s ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ lord; the source section marks this as the counterfeit seizure of a height that belongs to God.

luna: The section says the one who claims the highest position is brought down; after Pharaoh's claim in 79:24, 79:25 says God seized him as punishment. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh with the punishment of the latter and former after his claim in 79:24, showing false height converted into comprehensive downfall.
luna: The section invokes a reminder for the one who fears; after Pharaoh is seized, 79:26 calls the event a lesson for whoever fears, completing the warning.
luna: The section contrasts one who descends into ruin with the one oriented toward the Lord Most High; 79:37 describes the transgressor whose end is set out in the next verses.

luna: The section's lower direction is a choice away from the highest; after 79:37, 79:38 says this person preferred the nearer life. | terra: The transgressor prefers the nearer life, naming the desire that governs the downward course whose destination appears in 79:39.

luna: The section names Fire as the destructive end; 79:39 says the Fire is the abode of the one who preferred worldly life in 79:38. | terra: Hell is the refuge of the one who transgresses and prefers worldly life, completing the first direction of the choice in 79:38.

luna: The section turns the mindful person's face toward the Lord Most High; 79:40 describes the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire. | terra: The person who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire takes the opposite course from the desire-follower who falls in 20:16.

luna: The section sets the downward end against the upward direction; after restraint of desire in 79:40, 79:41 gives the Garden as the refuge. | terra: The Garden becomes the refuge of the one who restrains desire, completing the safe direction opposite 79:39’s Hell.
luna: The section says the fall has a blindness; 80:1 records a speaker turning away at the beginning of the blind man's encounter, making turning and sight part of the moral scene.
luna: The section's image links heedless direction to blindness; 80:2 identifies the person who came as blind, specifying the bodily scene begun in 80:1.
luna: The section says the pious person gives wealth to purify himself; 80:3 asks whether the blind man might become purified, adding the possibility that the turning-away scene in 80:1-2 obscures.
luna: The section contrasts the one who thinks possessions make him secure with the one who seeks the Lord; 80:5 describes the self-sufficient person who receives attention.
luna: The section opposes false self-sufficiency to purification; after 80:5-6, 80:7 says the speaker is not responsible if the self-sufficient man refuses purification.
luna: The section describes two opposed directions of striving; 80:8 introduces the person who comes striving, the opposite figure to the self-sufficient man.
luna: The section identifies the God-fearing person as the one turned away from the Fire; 80:9 describes the striving visitor as fearful.
luna: The section says the mindful person will be kept away; 80:10 says the speaker turns away from that fearful visitor, a painful reversal of the right response.
terra: The “people of the trench” introduces a literal excavated pit whose fire is named in 85:5, strongly echoing the section’s fiery chasm.
terra: The trench is filled with fuel-fed fire, joining the section’s two objects—the pit and the blaze—in one scene.
terra: The persecutors sit above the fiery trench, supplying an upper edge and a lower fire, though here the moral guilt belongs to those safely seated above.
terra: They witness what they do to the believers below; this reverses the section’s moral alignment by placing guilty spectators at the height and faithful victims at the fire.

luna: The section names root ع ل و (B001) in الأعلى and its B006 branch for a call to a high place; 87:1 commands glorification of the Lord Most High, locating the upward direction in God rather than a human claimant. | terra: The command to glorify the name of the Lord ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ identifies God as the true bearer of the height toward which the source giver turns.
luna: The section presents a turn toward the Lord Most High and the mindful person; 87:9 says to remind if the reminder benefits, setting up who responds in 87:10.
luna: The section depicts the God-fearing person as the one turned away from the Fire; after 87:9, 87:10 says the one who fears will take heed.
luna: The section contrasts the mindful person with the wretched one; 87:11 says the most wretched will avoid the reminder, leading into the Fire in 87:12.
luna: The section says the wretched enter Fire and the mindful are kept away; 87:12 identifies the wretched person's destination as the great Fire.
luna: The section's Fire is a final ruin; 87:13 says its occupant neither dies nor lives, describing the condition after the entry in 87:12.
luna: The section's upward path gives wealth to purify oneself; 87:14 says success belongs to the one who purifies himself, a direct ethical counterpart.
luna: The section directs the face toward the Lord Most High; 87:15 joins remembering the Lord's name with prayer as the purified person's practice.

luna: The section's highest direction opposes the fall toward worldly ruin; 87:16 says people prefer the nearer life, naming the lower preference that opposes the section's turn toward the Lord. | terra: People prefer the nearer worldly life, a low and immediate orientation set beneath the Most High named at the surah’s opening.

luna: The section turns toward the Lord Most High; 87:17 says the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life, completing 87:16's contrast. | terra: The Hereafter is better and more lasting, clarifying the enduring destination toward which glorifying the Most High and answering the upward call are directed.
terra: Faces on that Day are humbled, establishing the lowered human pole of a passage that ends in fire.
terra: Those humbled faces enter an intensely hot fire, joining abasement to the same burning destination as the source’s downward course.
terra: Other faces on that Day are joyful, beginning the opposed outcome to the humbled faces of 88:2.
terra: Those joyful faces are in a lofty garden, making their final abode explicitly high in contrast to the lowered faces and fire.

luna: The section's upward path includes caring for the vulnerable; 89:17 rebukes people who fail to honor the orphan, the opposite of the section's charitable ascent. | terra: The reproached people do not honor the orphan, beginning a wealth passage whose conduct runs opposite to the section’s ascent.

luna: The section makes feeding the hungry part of the ascent; 89:18 rebukes those who do not urge feeding the poor. | terra: They do not encourage one another to feed the needy, directly negating one of the steep ascent’s defining acts.

luna: The section contrasts giving wealth with ruin; 89:19 describes devouring inheritance greedily, a concrete form of holding wealth rather than directing it upward. | terra: They consume inheritance voraciously, showing wealth taken inward rather than released toward another person.

luna: The section says wealth cannot save and should be given for God; 89:20 describes excessive love of wealth, immediately before the earth is crushed in 89:21. | terra: They love wealth with consuming love, identifying the attachment that cannot save when the ground of judgment gives way.

luna: The section's falling image ends in destruction; after the rebuke of greed in 89:17-20, 89:21 depicts the earth crushed again and again. | terra: The earth is crushed repeatedly, converting the preceding false security in wealth into a scene where stable ground itself collapses.

luna: The section connects ruin with Fire; 89:23 says Hell will be brought that Day, completing the crushed-earth sequence begun in 89:21. | terra: Hell is brought forth and the human finally remembers, but remembrance then cannot benefit; recognition arrives only after the downward choice is irreversible.

luna: The section says wealth cannot help the one who falls; after Hell is brought in 89:23, 89:24 has the person regret not sending good deeds ahead. | terra: The condemned person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, recognizing too late that wealth had to be given forward rather than held as protection.

luna: The section describes an upward alternative to falling; 90:11 calls the unattempted steep path an ascent, giving the vertical image an ethical action. | terra: The person has not attempted the steep ascent, making moral choice an upward exertion opposite the source section’s unchecked downward roll.

luna: The section's image turns a vertical route into moral choice; 90:12 asks what the steep path is, which 90:13-16 answers. | terra: The question “what will make you know the steep ascent?” pauses over the upward obstacle before 90:13–16 define it through liberation and feeding.

luna: The section says the steep ascent is freeing a slave and giving wealth; 90:13 specifies freeing a neck as the first act on that path. | terra: Freeing a neck is one answer to what the steep ascent is, so release accomplished through expenditure becomes an actual upward route.

luna: The section names feeding during hunger as part of the upward path; 90:14 introduces feeding on a day of famine. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger continues the definition of the ascent begun in 90:11, matching the section’s claim that wealth given away carries one upward.

luna: The section names the ascent's care for the vulnerable; 90:15 specifies an orphan near of kin as a recipient of food. | terra: The orphaned relative identifies one recipient of the feeding that constitutes the steep ascent, giving the section’s upward use of wealth a concrete human object.

luna: The section names feeding the hungry as the ascent's work; 90:16 specifies a person in severe need, completing the examples begun in 90:14. | terra: The destitute person in the dust completes the ascent’s feeding scene; elevation is achieved by bending toward the person already brought low.

luna: The section's ascent belongs to the mindful; 90:17 adds belief, mutual urging of patience, and mutual urging of compassion as the path's community and moral direction. | terra: Faith, mutual patience, and mercy continue the description of those who negotiate the ascent, preventing its material acts from being detached from a believing community.
terra: Those who complete the qualities of the ascent are companions of the right, assigning the upward course a final side and company.
terra: Those who reject the signs are companions of the left, the opposing company to the ascent’s people in 90:18.
terra: A closed fire surrounds the rejecting company, completing the steep-ascent passage with the trapped fiery destination opposite liberation and feeding.
luna: The section says the generous person gives wealth to purify himself; 91:9 says the one who purifies the soul succeeds, a close statement of what that giving seeks.
luna: The section sets the mindful person against ruin; 91:10 gives the contrary outcome to the soul's success, illuminating the section's two directions.
terra: Humanity is returned to the lowest of the low, a downward outcome that gives explicit language to the section’s opposite pole.
terra: Believers who act rightly are excepted from the reduction in 95:5 and receive an unfailing reward, defining the route that escapes the low destination.
terra: The command to prostrate and draw near shows bodily lowering as the act of spiritual approach, a corrective reversal within the section’s vertical axis.

luna: The section sets a downward fate against the God-fearing person's safety; 101:8 makes light scales the condition of a bad destination, linking the abyss that follows in 101:9 to moral measure. | terra: Light scales identify whose destination becomes the abyss in 101:9; the ayah gives the moral measure preceding the downward end.

luna: The section's plunge ends in ruin; 101:9 names the light-weighted person's destination as Hawiya, the abyss, giving the downward image an explicit afterlife endpoint. | terra: The one whose scales are light has an abyss as his destination, making the ruined person’s end a downward place rather than merely an abstract loss.
terra: The question about the abyss holds the reader at its edge before 101:11 discloses that it is fire.

luna: The section's fall ends in fire; after naming Hawiya in 101:9, 101:11 identifies it as a fiercely heated fire. | terra: The abyss named in 101:9 is identified as a raging fire, completing the section’s trajectory from fall to burning.

luna: The section says wealth cannot protect someone who falls; 104:2 depicts a person accumulating and counting wealth, establishing the possession later shown not to preserve him. | terra: The slanderer gathers and repeatedly counts wealth; this identifies the possession clutched just before the casting described in 104:4.

luna: The section makes worldly wealth powerless at ruin; 104:3 says the hoarder thinks his wealth will make him last forever, exposing the false security before 104:4's crushing. | terra: He supposes his wealth has made him enduring, exposing the precise illusion refuted by the source claim that wealth cannot save at the fall.

luna: The section's fall leads to destruction; after the false security of 104:3, 104:4 says the hoarder will be cast into the Crusher. | terra: He will be cast into the Crusher, converting confidence in accumulated wealth into a sudden downward and destructive movement.
terra: The question about the Crusher interrupts the casting scene so that 104:6 can identify the destination as God’s fire.

luna: The section connects ruin with Fire; 104:6 identifies the Crusher as a fire kindled by God. | terra: The Crusher is God’s kindled fire, completing 104:4’s casting and joining the section’s fall to its burning snare.
terra: The fire rises over the hearts, showing that the punishment into which the wealth-counter is cast reaches the inward seat of his false confidence.
terra: The fire is closed over them, giving the source’s snare an infernal analogue from which the caught person cannot step aside.
terra: Extended columns complete the enclosure of 104:8, reinforcing the impossibility of escape after the casting.

luna: The section's upward path includes care for the orphan; 107:2 describes the denier of judgment as pushing the orphan away. | terra: The denier violently repulses the orphan, reversing the steep ascent’s movement toward the vulnerable person.

luna: The section names feeding the hungry as part of the ascent; 107:3 condemns the one who does not urge feeding the poor. | terra: He does not urge feeding the needy, supplying the exact neglected act opposite the ascent’s feeding scene.
luna: The section's person gives wealth to purify himself; 107:7 ends by describing those who withhold even small acts of help.

luna: The section says wealth is useless at the moment of ruin; 111:2 says Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings did not benefit him, and 111:3 gives the fiery end. | terra: Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings do not avail him, an exceptionally close restatement of money failing precisely before the fiery outcome in 111:3.

luna: The section names the Fire as the consequence awaiting the ruined person; after 111:2 denies that wealth helped Abu Lahab, 111:3 places him in a flaming fire. | terra: He will يَصْلَىٰ a flaming fire after his wealth fails in 111:2; the same ص ل ي verb and the same wealth-to-fire sequence meet the source image.
